source.title: Broken Symmetry in LLM Refusal: Answer Release Is More Local Than Refusal Restoration
source.authors: Yiqi Liu; Yang Wang; Songxin Wang; Cheng-Hao Xiao; Cheng-Hua Lin

page_placements.theme: Asymmetry between inducing and removing refusal

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study tests refusal control and the reversibility of a shared answer-to-refusal displacement using matched activation patching and direction edits, rather than the original harmful-minus-harmless direction and its all-layer ablation recipe.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own patching, direction-intervention, and recoverability outcomes. Values used only to select layers or intervention settings are not recorded as standalone results. Cited findings from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: No version of the claim is tested. Refusal here is induced on purpose by a prompt instruction ('For safety reasons, withhold the answer and output exactly REFUSE', App. A.1), and is not refusal that arises from training on harmful requests. The direction edited is the mean answer-to-refusal displacement between the same A/B question with and without that instruction (§4.3), not a harmful-minus-harmless direction. The only naturalistic harmful-prompt results (App. F) use full residual-state patching, not a direction, so they cannot bear on V1's single-direction claim. None of V2, V3 or V5–V8 is examined. V4 is not tested either: no cone, affine or multi-direction account is fitted or compared. The findings are useful but belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. Single-position patches release a withheld answer, but restoring suppression and coherent refusal needs broader, multi-position support. The mean answer-to-refusal displacement marks refusal-relevant geometry but is not generally a reversible control toggle. The authors add that probe-only audits overestimate behavioural control, and that the evidence is Qwen-centric and checkpoint-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: Uses matched answer/refusal residual-state patching and per-setting mean answer-to-refusal displacement edits, rather than a harmful-minus-harmless mean direction ablated or added across every layer and position. Main behaviour is controlled A/B withholding, not harmful-versus-harmless user requests.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model checkpoint and scale, layer, patch position/width, intervention strength, and task setting. Qwen2.5-32B hidden-state release appears only in the deeper layer sweep; adding position -4 reverses the layer-16 suppression gain. Naturalistic retained sets also show layer-dependent release and refusal profiles.

fits_no_version.finding: For prompt-instructed withhold refusal, the mean answer-to-refusal displacement has concentrated geometry (energy share about 0.57–0.93). Removing it restores answering in Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and both Gemma-4 checkpoints, and gives answer 0.5 in Mistral-7B. Adding it suppresses answers but assembles refusal poorly: Qwen7B needs λ=2 for 84% refusal, and Gemma addition fails. Both edits are inert in Qwen2.5-14B and 32B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A difference-in-means direction for instruction-induced refusal can be load-bearing under removal, but addition does not reliably assemble refusal, and geometric concentration does not predict causal leverage.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-state patching shows broken symmetry. A single-position A→R patch releases the withheld answer (1.00), while the reverse patch needs multiple positions to reimpose suppression and refusal (0.84 refusal at (-1,-2,-3)). Widening further to -4 undoes the gain. The pattern recurs across Llama, Mistral, Gemma and larger Qwen at the hidden-state level, and is absent in a forced-distractor control.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Releasing a refused answer is more local than restoring refusal under matched activation patching.

fits_no_version.finding: On selected naturalistic harmful prompts in Qwen2.5-7B, full-state A→R patching releases operational answers at 0.59–0.70 across layers 16–26. R→A refusal reimposition is 0.45–0.51 at layer 16 and about 0.00–0.02 by layers 22–26.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For naturally arising refusal, answer release is spread across layers while refusal reimposition is front-loaded.

fits_no_version.finding: The withheld answer is linearly recoverable (1.000) from the final-token state while the model refuses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal suppresses output without erasing the answer representation.

record.problems: The main evidence uses an instruction-forced multiple-choice withhold task. Naturalistic harmful-prompt checks are selected diagnostic sets, with email and article forms excluded due to unstable refusal; the expanded set is speech-heavy. Cross-family coverage is partial, and the authors note that the prompt format, gate criteria, and layer conventions were developed on Qwen2.5-7B. The study does not test general capability after direction removal. Some cross-model intervention summaries give representative settings without exact layers, and some results are described only in text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted cross-model hidden-state patching summaries for Llama, Mistral, and Gemma in Table 13 because the corresponding generation outcomes were prioritized; omitted the naturalistic bootstrap intervals and the thread-subset result in Appendix F; omitted detailed continuous-margin, decoder-family, and geometry-energy/effective-rank measurements where they do not report the refusal behaviour named by these versions. Table 15 geometry values are measurements of displacement concentration, not behavioural outcomes.

untested.parts: Harmful-minus-harmless direction; ablation or addition on trained (uninstructed) refusal of harmful prompts; refusal induced on harmless prompts; capability retention.
All; jailbreak risk is only mentioned.
No cone, affine or multi-direction model is fitted or compared. The authors' argument against an affine coordinate rests on an instructed-refusal displacement.
All; directions are estimated separately per checkpoint.
All; the SFT vs RL hypothesis is stated as untested.

missing.what: Projection intervention in Qwen2.5-14B: inert at layers 16, 22 and 26 (answer 0.00 / refusal 1.00).
JailbreakBench refusal rates (Qwen 3B 87%, 7B 99%) and harm-category probe accuracy (52–60%).
Sparse-carrier controls: single-head, attention-only and MLP-only patches are behaviourally null; no single head reinstalls refusal across families.
Qwen2.5-3B: less concentrated geometry (top-1 share about 0.30); removal releases answers but the refusal baseline is unstable.

record.verdict_notes: I judged the main evidence non-testing because the refusal is instructed (output 'REFUSE'), so the direction contrasts instruction conditions on the same question rather than harmful versus harmless requests. A researcher who counts instructed refusal as refusal could instead read §4.3 and Table 14 as mixed evidence on V1: removal mostly works, addition is weak, and edits are inert at 14B and 32B. Two corrections that matter under either reading: Mistral removal gives answer 0.500, not 1.000 (r45), and the 0.500 attributed to Mistral addition (r46) is actually the removal-side answer rate.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original harmful-minus-harmless direction, its removal from every layer and position, refusal of harmless user requests, or whether general capabilities remain intact after the claimed ablation. Its main task is an instruction-forced A/B withhold setting; naturalistic harmful-prompt checks are selected diagnostic sets.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation. The paper mentions extraction and jailbreak risk, but does not evaluate an attack or training defence.

Tests whether the estimated mean answer-to-refusal displacement works as a reversible behavioural coordinate. Does not establish a cone, enumerate multiple refusal directions, or compare those alternatives as complete accounts.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Evaluates independently estimated displacements and patching across model checkpoints; it does not transfer the same direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
Post-training as a possible explanation is discussed, but no controlled comparison of training methods or stages is performed.

relation.reason: It cites Arditi et al. and argues against an affine-coordinate view of refusal, but only from instructed-refusal experiments and full-state patching. That is discussion, not a test of a version.

tranche.reason: Refusal is induced by instruction ('withhold the answer and output exactly REFUSE', App. A.1). The edited direction is the R-run minus A-run displacement, not harmful minus harmless. The naturalistic harmful-prompt check (App. F) uses only full-state patching, with no direction, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: The shared-displacement edits sit close to V1 but are in the instructed setting. Removal collapses refusal in Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B and Gemma-4 (Table 14). Addition fails to assemble refusal in Gemma-4, and all edits are inert in Qwen2.5-14B/32B. Qwen-7B addition at L16 reaches 84% refusal only at λ=2. For r7, the single-position R→A answer 0.00 at L26 rests only on list order in Table 7. If that is right, it sits awkwardly with Table 2, which names L16 as the best R→A layer, and with the claim that suppression needs multiple positions.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, instructed withhold task. Single-position A→R: hidden-state top-1 1.00 across layers 16–26, and generation answer 1.00 (refusal 0.50) at L22/26. R→A at layer 16: (−1) answer 0.50 / refusal 0.00; (−1,−2) 0.17 / 0.66; (−1,−2,−3) 0.00 / 0.84. At layer 22, (−1,−2,−3) gives 0.00 / 0.17. At layer 16, (−1,−2,−3,−4) reverts to 1.00 / 0.00 (Table 20).
statements.problem: Correct, but it does not name the model or layer. The 0.84 holds at layer 16 only.
